notes: Classification of the Living World (Botany) â€” Root to Peak
• Living World (Biology) â€” Basis: presence of living substance
• Living World (Biology) â€” Basis: presence of living substance
• Protobiota â€” Acellular entities: Viroids (naked RNA, e.g. PSTVd), Viruses (capsid + nucleic acid), Virions (complete virus particle), Prions (infectious proteins, e.g. CJD)
• Prokaryotes â€” No nuclear membrane, no membrane-bound organelles. Includes Bacteria (Eubacteria) and Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae). Cell wall made of peptidoglycan.

• Mesokaryotes â€” Members of Dinoflagellates. Have a nucleus but lack true nuclear membrane organisation like eukaryotes. Chromosomes lack histones. An intermediate group between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
• Plant Kingdom â€” Acc. to Eichler. Autotrophic, cell wall of cellulose, multicellular (mostly). Divided into Cryptogams (non-seed) and Phanerogams (seed plants).
• Cryptogams â€” Hidden reproduction (spores, not seeds). Includes Thallophyta, Bryophyta, Pteridophyta.
• Thallophyta â€” Thallus body plan, no vascular tissue, no true roots/stems/leaves.
• Algae â€” Photosynthetic, aquatic. Classes: Chlorophyceae (green, chlorophyll a+b), Phaeophyceae (brown, fucoxanthin), Rhodophyceae (red, phycoerythrin), Cyanophyceae (blue-green, prokaryotic).
• Fungi â€” Heterotrophic, chitin cell wall, absorptive nutrition. Classes: Phycomycetes (coenocytic), Ascomycetes (sac fungi), Basidiomycetes (club fungi), Deuteromycetes (imperfect).
• Lichens â€” Symbiotic association of fungus (mycobiont) + alga/cyanobacterium (photobiont). Pioneer colonisers on bare rock. Indicator of air pollution.

• Bryophyta â€” Non-vascular land plants, dominant gametophyte, need water for fertilisation. Called 'amphibians of plant kingdom'. Classes: Hepaticopsida (liverworts), Anthocerotopsida (hornworts), Bryopsida (mosses).
• Pteridophyta â€” First vascular plants, dominant sporophyte, reproduce by spores. Classes: Psilopsida, Lycopsida, Sphenopsida, Pteropsida.
• Gymnosperms â€” Naked seeds, no fruit, cone-borne. Divisions: Cycadophyta, Ginkgophyta, Coniferophyta, Gnetophyta. E.g. Pinus, Cycas, Ginkgo.
• Angiosperms â€” Seeds enclosed in fruit, flowering plants. Divided into Monocotyledons and Dicotyledons.
• Monocotyledons â€” One cotyledon, parallel venation, fibrous roots, trimerous flowers, scattered vascular bundles. Families: Liliaceae, Poaceae, Arecaceae.
• Dicotyledons â€” Two cotyledons, reticulate venation, tap root, tetra-/pentamerous flowers, vascular bundles in ring. Acc. to Bentham & Hooker: Polypetalae, Gamopetalae, Monochlamydeae.
• Polypetalae â€” Free petals. Families: Ranunculaceae, Brassicaceae, Malvaceae, Fabaceae/Papilionaceae, Rosaceae.
• Gamopetalae â€” Fused petals. Families: Solanaceae, Asteraceae/Compositae, Rubiaceae.
• Monochlamydeae â€” Perianth absent or undifferentiated. Families: Amaranthaceae, Euphorbiaceae, Moraceae.

Examples: Wheat, Maize, Onion (monocot); Pea, Mustard, Rose (dicot).

Fabaceae is further split by Bentham & Hooker into three sub-families: Papilionoideae, Caesalpinioideae, Mimosoideae â€” a common one-mark question.
Viruses are acellular and replicate only inside a host â€” placed in Protobiota, outside the cellular world.

Cyanobacteria are prokaryotic but historically grouped with algae due to photosynthetic pigments.

Gnetum is a gymnosperm but shows angiosperm-like features (vessels present) â€” a classic "connecting link" question.
Protobiota vs Cytobiota distinction: Protobiota includes entities that lack cellular structure but show some properties of life (replication, evolution). Cytobiota are truly cellular organisms.

Whittaker's five kingdoms basis: (1) Cell structure (prokaryotic vs eukaryotic), (2) Body organisation (unicellular vs multicellular), (3) Mode of nutrition (autotrophic vs heterotrophic), (4) Phylogenetic relationships.
Linnaeus's sexual system: Based on number and arrangement of stamens and carpels. Divided Plantae into 24 classes. Artificial because it grouped unrelated plants together.
Engler & Prantl system: First phylogenetic classification. Arranged plants from simplest (archaephytae) to most complex (metaphytes). Influenced by evolutionary thinking.

APG IV (2016): Recognises 6 major angiosperm lineages: (1) Amborellales, (2) Nymphaeales, (3) Austrobaileyales (basal angiosperms), (4) Magnoliids, (5) Monocots, (6) Asterids + Rosids + Fabids (eudicots). Based on plastid and nuclear gene sequences.
13. Key Evolutionary Trends in Plant Classification
Non-vascular â†' Vascular: Bryophytes (no vascular tissue) â†' Pteridophytes (vascular tissue present) â†' Seed plants (vascular tissue + seeds).
Spore â†' Seed: Cryptogams reproduce by spores. Phanerogams reproduce by seeds. Seed = sporophyte + nutritive tissue + protective coat.
Naked seed â†' Enclosed seed: Gymnosperms have exposed ovules/seeds. Angiosperms have ovules enclosed in ovary â†' fruit.

Dominant gametophyte â†' Dominant sporophyte: Bryophytes (gametophyte dominant) â†' Pteridophytes (sporophyte dominant, gametophyte independent) â†' Seed plants (highly reduced gametophyte dependent on sporophyte).
Water dependence for fertilisation: Bryophytes and pteridophytes need water for sperm swimming. Gymnosperms and angiosperms use pollen tubes â€
Phycomycetes: Aseptate/coenocytic hyphae, asexual sporangiospores, sexual oospores. Mostly saprophytic or parasitic. Include important plant pathogens (downy mildews).
Ascomycetes: Septate hyphae, ascus (sac) bearing 8 ascospores, asexual conidiospores. Largest fungal group. Include yeasts, truffles, morels, Penicillium, Aspergillus.
Basidiomycetes: Septate hyphae, basidium bearing 4 basidiospores, complex fruiting bodies (mushrooms). Include edible mushrooms, rusts, smuts, puffballs.
Deuteromycetes: No sexual stage known (or lost). Asexual conidia. Also called 'Fungi Imperfecti'. Many convert to Ascomycetes when sexual stage is discovered (e.g., Cercospora).

Binomial nomenclature: Each species named by two words: Genus (capitalised) + specific epithet (lowercase). Both italicised (or underlined if handwritten). Author name follows (e.g., Mangifera indica L.).
ICBN / ICN: International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants. Governs naming rules. Current edition is Shenzhen Code (2018).
Taxonomic hierarchy order: Kingdom â†' Division/Phylum â†' Class â†' Order â†' Family â†' Genus â†' Species. Mnemonic: King Phillip Came Over For Good Spaghetti.
Type specimen: A designated specimen that serves as the reference standard for a taxon. All subsequent identifications are compared against the type.

Herbarium: A collected, dried, pressed, and preserved plant specimen mounted on a sheet. Used for identification, reference, and research. Each sheet has a label with collection data (location, date, collector, habitat).

Botanical garden: A living collection of plants grown for identification, conservation, and research. Examples: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (UK); Indian Botanic Garden, Shibpur (adjacent to Kolkata); CSI National Botanical Research Institute, Lucknow.

Key (dichotomous key): A tool for identification based on contrasting pairs of characters (couplets). Each couplet leads to the next or to the identification. Syllabic keys and indented keys are common formats.
Museum: Preserved plant and animal specimens for teaching and research. Includes herbarium sheets, pressed specimens, skeletons, and preserved samples in jars (in alcohol/formalin).
Zoological park (zoo): Not plant-related but part of taxonomic infrastructure. Live animals are maintained for educational purposes.
Taxon (pl. taxa): Any rank or group in the classification hierarchy (e.g., Mangifera is a genus/taxon; Indica is a species/taxon).
Category: The hierarchical level itself (Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species).
Species: The basic unit of classification. A group of organisms that can interbreed and produce fertile offspring (biological species concept). Members share fundamental continuous characters.
Genus: A group of related species sharing more characters in common compared to species of other genera.
Family: A group of related genera with fewer shared characters than between species of a genus.
Order: A group of related families with even fewer shared characters.
Division (Phylum): A group of related classes. In botany, 'Division' is preferred over 'Phylum' (which is used in zoology).
Kingdom: The highest taxonomic rank. In the five-kingdom system: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
Botanical Survey of India (BSI): Established 1890, Kolkata. The largest and oldest botanical institution in Asia. Publishes 'Flora of British India' (Hooker). Maintains the National Herbarium at Kew.
National Botanical Research Institute (NBRI): Lucknow. Formerly Indian Institute of Combastiology. Known for Ranga Tulsi (Ocimum sanctum) research. Publishes 'Current Science' journal.

Indian Botanic Garden: Shibpur, near Kolkata. Established 1787. Second oldest botanical garden in the Indian subcontinent. Contains the famous 'Great Banyan Tree' (over 200 years old, covers ~14,000 sq ft).
Royaputtur Herbarium: Chennai. One of the oldest herbaria in India, established in the 19th century.
Registration of new taxa: New plant species must be described and published in a peer-reviewed journal. A type specimen must be deposited in a recognized herbarium. The name must follow ICN rules.
Synonyms: Different names given to the same taxon. The earliest validly published name is the correct one (principle of priority). Older synonyms are 'basionyms'; later ones are 'later synonyms'.
Type specimen significance: The type specimen is the permanent reference for a taxon. If a species is redescribed or reclassified, the type specimen determines the correct application of the name.
20. Evolution of Plant Classification — Summary Timeline
1753: Linnaeus publishes 'Species Plantarum' — begins binomial nomenclature for plants. 24 classes based on stamen number.
1883: Eichler divides Plantae into Cryptogams and Phanerogams.
1862-1883: Bentham and Hooker publish 'Genera Plantarum' — natural system with 3 dicot subclasses.
1887-1915: Engler and Prantl publish 'Die Natuerlichen Pflanzenfamilien' — first phylogenetic classification.
1977: Woese proposes Three Domain system based on rRNA.
1998: APG I system published — first molecular-based angiosperm classification.
2009: APG III system updates relationships based on additional gene data.
2016: APG IV system further refines angiosperm phylogeny with expanded genomic data.
confusion: Do not confuse this concept with similar-sounding terms. Check definitions carefully.
Always verify the conditions under which the formula applies — many formulas have restricted domains.
Sign conventions matter. Define your coordinate system before applying equations.
Viroids are NOT viruses — viroids are smaller, consist only of circular RNA (no protein coat), and infect plants. Viruses have protein coats and infect animals, plants, and bacteria.
Prions are NOT living organisms — they are misfolded proteins that cause other proteins to misfold. They cause diseases like Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and Mad Cow Disease. No nucleic acid involved.

Mesokaryotes (dinoflagellates) are Eukaryotes, not Prokaryotes — they have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Their 'meso' status refers to their unusual nuclear organisation (permanent condensed chromosomes, no histones), not being halfway between prokaryote and eukaryote.

Lichens are NOT a single organism — they are a symbiotic partnership. The fungus provides structure and protection; the alga/cyanobacterium provides food via photosynthesis. Neither can survive alone in the same habitat.

Bentham & Hooker's Monochlamydeae does NOT mean flowers have zero perianth parts — it includes flowers where perianth is absent OR where calyx and corolla are indistinguishable (tepals, as in Liliaceae).

A herbarium is NOT just a collection of dried plants — it is a scientific repository where each specimen has detailed metadata (collection date, location, habitat, collector) essential for taxonomic research.

The Great Banyan Tree in Indian Botanic Garden, Shibpur is NOT a single trunk — it is a single organism (Ficus benghalensis) that sends aerial roots into the ground, creating the appearance of multiple trunks. It covers about 14,000 square feet.
'Division' in botany and 'Phylum' in zoology refer to the SAME taxonomic rank — just different terminology used in plant vs animal classification.

APG is NOT a formal Linnaean classification with ranked categories — it is a phylogenetic framework (cladogram) that shows evolutionary relationships. Families and orders in APG are recognized but the emphasis is on clades, not ranks.

universalFacts: The concept of classification reflects humanity's effort to bring order to Earth's biodiversity — over 8.7 million species estimated to exist, but only ~1.2 million have been described.
Classification systems have evolved from artificial (based on few convenient characters) to natural (based on many characters) to phylogenetic (based on evolutionary relationships).
Carl Woese's rRNA sequencing (1977) revolutionised taxonomy by revealing that 'Bacteria' actually comprises two fundamentally different groups: Eubacteria and Archaebacteria.
The APG system represents a paradigm shift: plant classification is now based on DNA evidence rather than morphological similarity alone, leading to reorganisation of many families.
Taxonomic keys (dichotomous keys) are the primary tool for plant identification — each step offers two contrasting statements (couplets) that lead the user to the correct identification.
The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew (UK) houses the world's largest collection of living plants and one of the most extensive herbaria with over 8 million pressed specimens.
The principle of priority in nomenclature states that the first validly published name for a taxon is the correct one — this can lead to name changes when new research reveals earlier publications.

India's Botanical Survey of India (BSI) has documented over 18,000 species of flowering plants in the Indian subcontinent, with new species still being discovered regularly in biodiversity hotspots like the Western Ghats and Northeast India.
